questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ for $x\le 0$ and $y\ge 0,$ between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/8dc4ea0ad2bb776fb31132e1ff8d97efdd2c166dc23ffbc8641f8d7034b8d487.png)

The region $R$ is one-quarter of a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}=\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\text{d}V & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}r\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ between the surfaces $z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and $z=3.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/9c4ea0ba92e19a201e3944defa6deb0bc1ee76971adaa809521722b6ac31241f.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=r,$ and

- bounded above by $z=3.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,\,r\le z\le 3\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}r\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{r}^{3}{r}^{2}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
If the solid region $R$ is given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+(y-4)^{2}\le 16,\,x\ge 0,\,-5\le z\le x\},
$$

then ${∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}V=$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/b66b8db18b2f5773addc2d00c02f2f15f4a7ead53323418e63bd50457f74466b.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $4$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,4)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=-5,$ and

- bounded above by $z=x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=16$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =16 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -4)^{2} & =16 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -8r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +16 & =16 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-8r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-8r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,-5\le z\le r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1}\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+1}\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\int }_{-5}^{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r\sqrt{{r}^{2}+1}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=4-x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/62abd56d2d374afb7c608aa64f701cfe94f096b823f964697a929c7c24f3a073.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=4-x=4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,\,0\le z\le 4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}({(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2})\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}[z]_{z=0}^{z=4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}(4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}4{r}^{3}-{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[{r}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}_{r=0}^{r=1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[\theta -\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{5}(0-0) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}(x-y)\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3$ for $x\ge 0$ and between the surfaces $z=x$ and $z=9+x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/e289cfbd210112a619018a7b905f7f2b1a9859ecb84b2517dd745705624d79d7.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{3}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ and

- bounded above by $z=x+9=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta <\frac{\pi }{2},\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le z\le r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(x-y)\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )[z]_{z=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{z=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}9{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}[3{r}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )]_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}3(\sqrt{3})^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}9\sqrt{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =9\sqrt{3}[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =-\pi /2}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =9\sqrt{3}(1-(-1))+9\sqrt{3}(0-0) \\  & =18\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Cylindrical Solid
canonical_examples.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ for $y \geq 0$ between the surfaces $z =0$ and $z = 10 - x.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R y \:\textrm{d}V
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/9ad0d507a5440cfce9595e9054457fd733ae412d9a57b0a85238b4773ff0a0c7.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $2$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=10-x = 10 - r\cos\theta.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 10-r\cos\theta \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
If the solid region $R$ is given by 

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \, : \, (x-1)^2 + y^2 \leq 1, \: -2 \leq z \leq 4-y \right\},
$$

then express the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \: \textrm{d}V
$$

as an equivalent integral in cylindrical polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/a551e379767395a2422f690a66fc38defab64cff03c752c0c9a5a0748561d2f7.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(1,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z = -2,$ and

- bounded above by $z = 4 - y = 4 - r\sin{\theta}.$

With that in mind, let's write the equation $(x-1)^2 + y^2 = 1$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r = 2\cos{\theta}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 2\cos{\theta}, \: -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: -2 \leq z \leq 4-r\sin{\theta} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\int }_{-2}^{4-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating a Triple Integral by Converting to Cylindrical Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x+2y \:\textrm{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=5$ for $x\geq 0,$ $y\geq 0$ and between the surfaces $z=y$ and $z=y+3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/b7b37ffe8e97ed4a661ee98750894641c6ed3354864dd5b54d2ed076e4fdb69b.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{5}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=y=r\sin\theta,$ and

- bounded above by $z=y+3=r\sin\theta + 3.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq \sqrt{5}, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: r\sin\theta \leq z \leq r\sin\theta + 3\right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x+2y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{\int }_{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )[z]_{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}3{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{r}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )]_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{5}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{(\sqrt{5})}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}5\sqrt{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =5\sqrt{5}[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =5\sqrt{5}(1-0)-10\sqrt{5}(0-1) \\  & =15\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We can evaluate triple integrals by changing the variables to cylindrical polar coordinates.

For example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the finite region enclosed between the surfaces $z =0$ and $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/a63e349d2776fe07077379b9d603e32ad2ff264cfa8005a226422b44f7e100fe.png)

 

This is a challenging integral to evaluate as it currently stands. However, we should recognize that the problem naturally lends itself to cylindrical polar coordinates.

Recall that if $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/b2f8a6fe7f21b062eec294522e411c1e471b564eae68763d4767f917d65b54b0.png)

Notice that the region $R$ is

- bounded below by $z = 0,$ and

- bounded above by $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2 = 1 - r^2.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 1-r^2 \right\}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/dae76df462a695e655ffdde01559d19bf245aa6d601100fb8c7bc1024106a4c8.png)

 

To express our integral in terms of cylindrical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula, given by

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, {\color{blue}\mathrm{d}V} = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.
$$

When expressing our integral in cylindrical polar coordinates, we must write 

$$
{\color{blue}{\textrm{d}V}} = {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.
$$

It's important not to forget the extra factor of ${\color{blue}{r}}.$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{r}^{2}}{r}^{3}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
\int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1}} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1 - r^2 }} \bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black} r^3} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta
=
\dfrac{\pi}{6}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.
$$

tutorials.name: Deriving the Volume Element in Cartesian Coordinates
tutorials.problem:
Let's now build some intuition behind the meaning of the volume element $\textrm d V.$ This will help us to understand the change of variables formula in cylindrical polar coordinates. We start by considering the usual rectangular coordinate system.

Suppose we have a point $P$ and a neighboring point $Q$ in the Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/2535744585beb7fed89d760c0290a04f54d0a08c8f7e564b17c8e42432da031e.png)

 

Imagine moving from $P$ to $Q$ as follows:

- First, we move a distance $\textrm d x$ parallel to the $x$-axis so that the new point $P'$ has the same $x$-coordinate as $Q.$

- Then, we move a distance $\textrm d y$ parallel to the $y$-axis so that the new point $P''$ has the same $y$-coordinate as $Q.$

- Finally, we move a distance $\textrm d z$ parallel to the $z$-axis to land to $Q.$

These movements span the rectangular solid shown above. The volume of this solid, denoted $\textrm d V,$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{d}V = \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y \, \mathrm{d}z.
$$

Thus, the element $\textrm d V$ represents the volume generated by moving from the point $P$ to the point $Q$ in this coordinate system.

tutorials.name: Deriving the Volume Element in Cylindrical Polar Coordinates
tutorials.problem:
Let's now repeat this process for a cylindrical polar system. Consider the points $P$ and $Q$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/243d720546357a33eac3f96b84755cf6aeebafdef3a3672a3d29989147f134c2.png)

 

Imagine moving from $P$ to $Q$ as follows:

- First, we move a distance $\textrm d r$ so that the new point $P'$ has the same $r$-coordinate as $Q.$

- Then, we sweep through an angle $\textrm d \theta$ so that the new point $P''$ has the same $\theta$-coordinate as $Q.$ The arc length traced out by this movement approximately equals $r\,\textrm d \theta.$

- Finally, we move a distance $\textrm d z$ vertically to land on $Q.$

These three movements trace out a solid that's approximately rectangular, and so the approximate volume of this solid is given by

$$
\mathrm{d}V = \mathrm{d}r \cdot r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \cdot \mathrm{d}z=  r\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta.
$$
